                <jats:p>
                  Every year biotechnology labs generate a combined total of ∼5.5 million tons of plastic waste. As the global bioeconomy expands, biofoundries will inevitably increase plastic consumption in-step with synthetic biology scaling. Decontamination and reuse of single-use plastics could increase sustainability and reduce recurring costs of biological research. However, throughput and variable cleaning quality make manual decontamination impractical in most instances. Automating single-use plastic cleaning with liquid handling robots makes decontamination more practical by offering higher throughput and consistent cleaning quality. However, open-source, validated protocols using low-cost lab robotics for effective decontamination of plasticware—facilitating safe reuse—have not yet been developed. Here we introduce and validate TidyTron: a library of protocols for cleaning micropipette tips and microtiter plates that are contaminated with DNA,
                  <jats:italic>E. coli</jats:italic>
                  , and
                  <jats:italic>S. cerevisiae</jats:italic>
                  . We tested a variety of cleaning solutions, contact times, and agitation methods with the aim of minimizing time and cost, while maximizing cleaning stringency and sustainability. We tested and validated these cleaning procedures by comparing fresh versus cleaned tips and plates for contamination with cells, DNA, or cleaning solutions. We assessed contamination by measuring colony forming units by plating, PCR efficiency and DNA concentration by qPCR, and event counts and debris by flow cytometry. Abstract:
Efficient and consistent DNA extraction is crucial for genotyping but often hindered by the limitations of traditional manual processes, which are labour-intensive, error-prone, and costly. We introduce a semi-automated, robotic-assisted DNA extraction (RoboCTAB) tailored for large-scale plant genotyping, leveraging advanced yet affordable liquid-handling robotic systems. The protocol/workflow integrates a CTAB extraction protocol specifically adapted for a robotic liquid-handling system, making it compatible with high-throughput genotyping techniques such as SNP genotyping and sequencing. Various plant parts (leaves, roots, manual seed chip) were explored as the source material for DNA extractions, with the aim of identifying the tissue best suited for collection on a large scale. Young roots (radicle) proved the easiest to harvest at scale, while the harvest of leaves and seed chips were more laborious and error-prone. DNA yield and quality from both leaves and roots (but not seed chips) were similar and sufficient for downstream analysis. Interestingly, root tissue could still be extracted from imbibed seeds, even if the seeds failed to germinate, thus proving useful for DNA extraction. Cost analysis indicates significant savings in labour costs, highlighting the approach’s suitability for large-scale projects. Quality assessments demonstrate that the robotic process yields high-quality DNA, maintaining integrity for downstream applications. This semi-automated DNA extraction system represents a scalable, reliable solution for large-scale genotyping that is accessible to many users who cannot implement highly sophisticated and costly systems as are known to exist in large multinational seed companies. RoboCTAB, a low-cost, optimized method for high-throughput DNA extraction, minimizes the risk of cross-contamination. RoboCTAB is capable of processing up to four 96-well plates (384 samples) simultaneously in a single run, improving cost-efficiency and providing seamless integration with laboratory workflows, potentially setting new standards for efficiency and quality in DNA processing and sequencing at scale.

The excerpt supports the cost and conceptual framing of low-cost laboratory automation. It identifies the Opentrons OT-2 as having an approximately USD 7,500 starting cost, while noting that whether it counts as consumables, spare resources, or dedicated support depends on the institution and use case. The review defines a “frugal twin” as a low-cost counterpart to a higher-cost physical laboratory system. Frugal twins are intended to provide lower-risk environments for rapid prototyping and education, while offering insights relevant to more expensive systems. Their usefulness lies on a trade-off spectrum between cost and research capability. Cost reduction can be achieved either by reducing capabilities or by accepting lower accuracy and precision; the appropriate balance depends on available resources and required functions. Table 1 lists a “Cheap automated synthesis platform” for chemistry and organic synthesis at an estimated cost of USD 450, illustrating that a component or platform-level low-cost estimate can be substantially below the OT-2 starting price. The excerpt does not provide the requested later-source results concerning OT-2 protein throughput, AutoLab adoption, cell-culture labor savings, OT-Mation CSV-to-Python workflows, integration standards, or specific bill-of-materials versus all-in cost distinctions. It therefore supports only the OT-2, frugal-twin, and USD 450 platform portions of the requested comparison.

Abstract

Self-driving laboratories (SDLs) are rapidly outgrowing the single-instrument prototype, scaling
into multi-instrument and multi-site platforms that run autonomous discovery across chemistry,
materials science, biotechnology, pharmaceutical re-search and adjacent domains. What now decides
whether an SDL can scale, share its integrations and federate experiments is no longer the algorithms
or the robots, but the software layer that orchestrates heterogeneous devices. Today that layer is
the bottleneck: a fast-growing ecosystem of open-source orchestrators in which most have built
device integration on their own bespoke conventions instead of adopting a formally governed
standard. The result is predictable and costly. Integrations do not transfer between laboratories,
orchestrators cannot interoperate and many new SDLs rebuild their device-control layer from
scratch. Crucially, this is an engineering coordination problem, not a fundamental scientiﬁc one
and therefore among the most tractable bottlenecks in autonomous science. We map the device-
integration standards landscape onto the open-source orchestrator ecosystem, compare the leading
options and give scenario-driven guidance on when to use each. We then translate the requirements
of autonomous operation into a concrete deliverable: a set of testable engineering criteria and a
weighted procurement scorecard that deﬁnes an autonomous-ready control interface and gives
institutional buyers the leverage to demand it; these requirements do not change as orchestration
turns agentic: whether an instrument is driven by a program or by a language-model agent through a
model-facing protocol, it is only as safe and reliable as the interface it exposes. Adopted at scale, these
requirements turn device integration from a burden repaid lab by lab into shared infrastructure,

function.arguments:
{"answer": "# Laboratory automation and self-driving laboratories: market evidence

**Bottom line.** There is a substantial, established market for *clinical* laboratory automation, but it should not be presented as the market for research self-driving laboratories (SDLs). The accessible market reports and studies document growing research activity, operating cloud labs, and useful commercial instruments; they do **not** establish a defensible stand-alone global SDL revenue figure, SDL growth rate, or profitability for the named private companies. (pqac-00000019, pqac-00000020, pqac-00000000, pqac-00000025)

## Size, growth, and the measurement boundary

Nam and Park’s 2025 clinical-laboratory review puts the **2023 global total laboratory automation (TLA) systems market at US$5.57–6.1 billion**. TLA here means automation across clinical specimen handling, testing, and post-analytical processes—not AI-directed research experiments. Their references identify a **QYResearch report updated June 2024**, covering 2024–2030, and a **Precedence Research report updated August 2024**, covering 2024–2034. The accessible material does not reproduce a verifiable forecast dollar value or CAGR from those reports; assigning one to the SDL segment would be unjustified. (pqac-00000019, pqac-00000020)

The same review reports **115 South Korean institutions operating TLA in 2024**, including **36 of 47 tertiary hospitals (77%)** and **58 of 331 general hospitals (18%)**. Its market-share figure puts **North America at 38%** and depicts **Siemens, Roche, and Beckman Coulter at 34%, 31%, and 25%**, respectively, in the reported clinical-automation vendor breakdown. These illustrate adoption and concentration within the *clinical* category, not an SDL company ranking. (pqac-00000019, pqac-00000050)

Research activity is growing, but it is a different metric: Jung and colleagues analyzed **352 SDL papers published during 2004–2023** and found a marked rise after **2019**. A 2025 study surveying publicly identifiable cloud labs found **15 example organizations worldwide**, explicitly **not** an exhaustive census. Neither publications nor provider counts measure revenue. (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000032, pqac-00000034)

The following comparison keeps market revenue, research activity, access commitments, and equipment prices separate.

<artifact id="artifact-00"/>

## How the businesses capture value

* **Instruments and integration.** Manufacturers sell liquid handlers, modules, analytical instruments, consumables, and support. A robot is not itself an SDL: experiment-selection algorithms, instrument interfaces, scheduling, measurements, and data infrastructure must close the loop. In 2024, Roche researchers integrated an **Opentrons OT-2** with their in-house **AutoLab** orchestration software using the robot’s API, illustrating why instrument sales and the integration/software layer are distinct sources of value. (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000041, pqac-00000045)
* **Software.** Protocol-generation, orchestration, sample tracking, analysis, and data management can be developed internally, distributed openly, or supplied commercially. The open-source **OT-Mation** project, published in **2025**, converts experimental-design CSV files into executable OT-2 Python protocols; it demonstrates a software complement to purchased hardware, not evidence of software-market revenue. (pqac-00000039)
* **Cloud labs and services.** A provider operates expensive physical facilities while customers remotely specify experiments and obtain measurements and records; charges may combine access commitments and usage. Academic authors distinguish **Emerald Cloud Lab’s (ECL’s)** broad instrument-access approach from **Strateos’s** predefined workflows emphasizing drug discovery and synthetic biology. A 2025 review reports an **ECL minimum financial commitment exceeding US$250,000**, but this secondary-source figure is not independently verified pricing or ECL revenue. Moving capital spending from customer to provider does not eliminate infrastructure or operating costs. (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000010, pqac-00000015, pqac-00000024)

## What happened at the named companies

**Emerald Cloud Lab.** A 2025 cloud-lab landscape report lists ECL’s Austin facility at **105,000 ft² and more than 230 instruments**; it lists the ECL–Carnegie Mellon facility at **20,000 ft² and more than 200 instruments**. Its **2021** CMU entry refers to the announced project, **not proof that it was fully operational in 2021**. More concretely, a **2025** published study remotely performed copper-nanocluster experiments at ECL in Austin and CMU’s automated laboratory in Pittsburgh, using different handlers and spectrometers across sites; models trained on **40 samples** predicted successful synthesis. This demonstrates research use and cross-site validation, not ECL profitability or a measured company-wide productivity gain. (pqac-00000025, pqac-00000029, pqac-00000021)

**Strateos/Transcriptic.** Strateos emerged from the **Transcriptic–3Scan merger**; the landscape report lists a **14,000-ft² facility and approximately 200 instruments** under its **2019** company entry. Its original remote, workflow-oriented offering was followed by an announced shift toward **on-site cloud labs**, reported in academic discussion in **2024**. A substantive operating example is the DARPA SD2 *Round Trip* project: its open software was integrated with the **Strateos robotic cloud laboratory** and, by the **2022** paper, had been applied to **nearly 100 experiments**. The authors report roughly **two orders of magnitude faster experimental design and analysis** than prior ad hoc processes and describe a project-workflow staffing comparison of approximately **ten versus three people**. Those are results for the **combined software and experimental workflow**; they do not isolate a Strateos-only effect or establish Strateos revenue, margins, or profitability. (pqac-00000025, pqac-00000024, pqac-00000028, pqac-00000035, pqac-00000036)

**Opentrons.** Its commercially sold, programmable OT-2 offers a lower-cost route to *in-house* automation rather than remote access to a provider’s lab. Published indicative prices differ with date and configuration: approximately **US$7,500 starting cost** in a **2024** review; about **US$10,000** as a **2025** review’s entry-level estimate; and approximately **US$20,000–30,000** with pipettes and accessory modules for a **2024** protein-workflow study. In that study, researchers processed **96 proteins in parallel**, with a proposed capacity of hundreds per user per week. These are product and application figures, **not** Opentrons sales, market share, or profits. (pqac-00000044, pqac-00000015, pqac-00000042)

The industrial economics are instructive. Roche’s **2024** OT-2/AutoLab study reports **30 minutes less hands-on work per MetID assay**, approximately **half the labor cost per sample**, agreement with manual results of **ICC 0.998**, and replicate variability averaging **less than one-third** of the manual procedure’s. Nevertheless, at the studied assay volume the authors say the labor saving **did not fully offset hardware usage within five years**; sharing the machine across workflows might improve payback. This is stronger evidence than assuming every affordable robot rapidly pays for itself. (pqac-00000045)

The landscape report cautions that provider facility measurements can include offices, instrument counts are reported inconsistently, and much information comes from company statements. The retrieved evidence supplies **no independently verified annual revenue, customer counts, profitability, valuation outcome, or definitive exit outcome** for ECL, Strateos, or Opentrons. Facility scale, funding or a published experiment should not be substituted for those business outcomes. (pqac-00000025, pqac-00000032, pqac-00000033)

## Open source: adoption benefits and cost limits

Open designs and code let labs modify instruments, share protocols, and build applications atop a purchased platform. Illustrations include the **2025** OT-Mation software; the **2025** open-source OT-2 cell-culture system that cut hands-on plate-passaging time by **more than half** in its reported tests; and a **2025** review’s account of the 3D-printed **FINDUS** liquid handler costing **under US$400 to construct**. The latter is a *construction* figure, not a like-for-like quotation for a validated, serviced commercial workstation. A 2024 review also describes a roughly **US$450** educational synthesis platform as a “frugal twin”: useful for learning and prototyping, but potentially less capable or precise than the research system it approximates. (pqac-00000039, pqac-00000049, pqac-00000047, pqac-00000009)

Openness does not remove the cost of calibration, skilled integration, analytical instruments, consumables, quality control, or maintenance. Roche notes the OT-2’s limited deck space, absence of plate transport and liquid-level detection, and eight-channel maximum head. A **2026 preprint** further argues that incompatible instrument-control conventions cause labs to rebuild integrations even when orchestration software is open source. Thus, open hardware and software plausibly lower the **entry price and reuse cost**, while validated interoperability and sufficient instrument utilization determine whether they lower the **cost per reliable result**. (pqac-00000041, pqac-00000009, pqac-00000048, pqac-00000045)

**Assessment:** The demonstrated opportunity spans several different businesses—clinical automation equipment, research instruments, workflow software, and experiment-as-a-service. Published case studies substantiate technical utility and some workflow savings. They do **not**, on the evidence available here, substantiate a precise SDL market CAGR or the financial success of the three private companies. (pqac-00000019, pqac-00000000, pqac-00000025, pqac-00000045)"}

These illustrate adoption and concentration within the *clinical* category, not an SDL company ranking. (nam2025revolutionizinglaboratorypractices pages 2-4, nam2025revolutionizinglaboratorypractices media 099f385e)

A 2025 study surveying publicly identifiable cloud labs found **15 example organizations worldwide**, explicitly **not** an exhaustive census. Neither publications nor provider counts measure revenue. (jung2025researchtrendanalysis pages 25-26, zilgalvis2025yingchiangjeffreylee pages 12-14, zilgalvis2025yingchiangjeffreylee pages 9-12)

(2025) (doloi2025democratizingselfdrivinglabs pages 6-7) |

contexts.context: The excerpt provides a concrete experimental outcome involving Emerald Cloud Lab (ECL), rather than a promotional projection. Researchers remotely programmed and executed copper nanocluster synthesis at ECL in Austin and Carnegie Mellon University’s Automated Science Lab in Pittsburgh. The study used different liquid handlers and spectrometers across the two independent facilities, thereby testing whether results were reproducible across sites and instruments. The authors report that the multi-instrument setup controlled reaction parameters and reduced operator- and instrument-specific variability. Using a dataset of only 40 training samples, interpretable machine-learning models predicted whether synthesis parameters would produce copper nanoclusters, with SHAP analysis offering mechanistic interpretation. The paper frames cross-site validation and reproducibility as outcomes relevant to reliable ML-driven materials discovery. However, this excerpt does not report ECL’s operating dates, CMU’s broader operational or academic project portfolio, pricing, minimum spending, revenue, profitability, or other commercial metrics. It also contains no information about Strateos/Transcriptic, the 3Scan merger, the 2023 onsite pivot, Strateos enzyme-engineering or DARPA SD2 results, or Opentrons’ Roche adoption and performance. Thus, the evidence here supports a measured ECL-linked cross-laboratory research result, but not conclusions about business success or financial performance.

The system used modular protocols, spreadsheets, generated Python scripts, and packaged software dependencies; users did not need coding expertise. Cross-laboratory validation reduced operator/instrument variability; interpretable ML predicted copper-nanocluster formation from only 40 training samples. Spectra were recorded every 43 seconds for 80 minutes. The authors note conventional ML datasets may require “hundreds or thousands of experiments,” motivating automation. This excerpt contains no market-size, growth, business-model, Opentrons, Strateos/Transcriptic, or open-source adoption/cost data.

It distinguishes researcher-driven cloud labs, where scientists retain control of experimental design and decisions, from self-driving cloud labs, where AI and algorithms manage experiments, analyze data, and make decisions. contexts.context: This excerpt is from Bryce et al., “Round Trip: An Automated Pipeline for Experimental Design, Execution, and Analysis,” published in ACS Synthetic Biology on January 31, 2022 (received July 2, 2021). It describes the DARPA SD2 Round Trip (RT) software architecture, an open architecture intended to automate key Test and Learn activities in high-throughput laboratory science. Its central contribution is automated metadata creation, curation, standardization, and linkage with experimental data, supporting faster and more reproducible analysis. The article reports that the RT sped up experiment design and analysis by two orders of magnitude compared with prior ad hoc methods, and Figure 1 contrasts conventional collaboration taking many weeks with RT-supported workflows taking hours. The excerpt states that SD2 involved approximately 100 researchers and that many challenge-problem demonstrations used RT, but it does not establish that nearly 100 experiments were conducted. It also provides no ten-to-three staff reduction, no quantified separation of software effects from Strateos/cloud-lab effects, and no information about the 2025 RAND/Zilgalvis survey, provider count, ECL Austin, CMU, or Strateos facility sizes and instrument counts. Those claims require the separate 2025 report and additional sections of the Bryce article.

contexts.context: This excerpt provides evidence for Roche’s 2024 deep integration of an Opentrons OT-2 with AutoLab and open-source networking tools, but it does not report the specific component or total-cost figures requested for Lo et al. (2024), Doloi et al. (2025), or 3D-printing-based systems. The OT-2 is characterized as a low-price, cost-effective platform for low-throughput assays. In the MetID deployment, automation reduced hands-on time by 30 minutes per assay and was estimated to halve labor cost per sample, although hardware usage was not fully offset within a five-year period. The authors note that deploying multiple workflows on one machine and reusing BPMN components and Python code could accelerate break-even and workflow development. The integrated workflow retrieved information from Roche databases, stored outputs on the Roche network, supported modular protocols and global variable passing, and enabled inline data analysis and database saving. Biological validation showed high agreement with manual execution (intraclass correlation coefficient 0.998), while replicate coefficient of variation was less than one-third of the manual procedure. The excerpt supports adoption and integration benefits, but it does not provide OT-2 throughput of 96, exact hardware prices such as $7,500 or $10,000, frugal-twin costs, high-end-platform comparisons in dollar terms, ECL minimum costs, or detailed integration-standard limitations.

contexts.context: Norton-Baker et al. (2024) describe a low-cost, robot-assisted pipeline for high-throughput protein expression and purification using small-scale E. coli cultures and an affordable liquid-handling robot. The system processes 96 proteins in parallel, with minimal waste, and is scalable to hundreds of proteins per user per week. Replicate experiments produced reproducible protein purity and yields of up to 400 µg, sufficient for thermostability and activity analyses. The excerpt provides context for distinguishing equipment acquisition costs from complete bill-of-materials or all-in costs: commercial Hamilton and Tecan systems with necessary capabilities were reported as costing more than $150,000, KingFisher systems processing 96 samples about $80,000, while an Opentrons OT-2 equipped with pipettes and accessory modules was estimated at approximately $20,000–30,000 at the time of writing. Miniaturization reduces material cost and waste per sample, but introduces practical limitations, including culture aeration, cross-well contamination, low-volume transfer losses, adequate final protein concentration, and downstream buffer compatibility. This excerpt does not provide the other requested studies’ prices, adoption results, software integrations, or standards.

contexts.context: Moukarzel et al. (2024) demonstrate adoption of the open-source Opentrons OT-2 for automated Bradford protein and PicoGreen double-stranded-DNA assays. The instrument met the stated assay acceptance criteria, including reference-curve fits above R² 0.98, replicate precision limits, back-calculation error below 15%, and system-suitability results within control limits. Back-calculated concentrations agreed with those from a Tecan EVO, with all platform differences within −20% to 20%. The OT-2 reduced runtime relative to manual execution, although it was somewhat slower than the Tecan because it lacks a 96-channel head for bulk transfers and reagent additions. The article identifies the system’s small footprint, low cost, user-friendly interface, and Python programmability as major advantages. Python scripts can specify sample and well locations, add samples, and automatically transfer plate contents. However, this excerpt provides no numerical component bill of materials or all-in acquisition cost, so it cannot substantiate specific prices such as $7,500 or $450. Reported limitations include programming requirements, workflow compatibility constraints, no robotic arm or plate gripper, manual transfer to the plate reader, no automatic liquid detection, and no emergency stop; these necessitate operator supervision and distinguish the OT-2 from fully integrated systems.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides evidence for an open-source software contribution around the Opentrons OT-2, but it does not report purchase prices, component bills of materials, total system costs, adoption counts, throughput figures, or comparative cost results. Laverick et al. describe OT-Mation as an open-source Python script that converts four user-defined CSV files into bespoke OT-2 Python protocols. The files specify deck labware, reagents, pipetting hardware, and experimental-design parameters; typically, only the Experimental Parameters file must change between experiments. The software is intended to connect multifactorial design-of-experiments outputs with executable liquid-handling code, reducing manual GUI or code entry. Claimed benefits include improved reproducibility, reduced human error, streamlined workflows, and support for researchers with limited programming skills. Its design supports iterative workflows, automated dilution calculations from stock to target concentrations, and a broad range of reagent commands, making it applicable beyond DoE to serial dilutions and PCR setup. Generated scripts can be archived with experimental data as records of completed experiments. The implementation was developed in Python 3.7 and 3.9, reported as running in Python 3.12 on Windows and macOS, and tested on an Opentrons OT-2. No information in this excerpt addresses integration standards or limitations in detail.

contexts.context: This excerpt provides a concrete total workstation cost and adoption/performance evidence for the Opentrons OT-2, but it does not provide a component bill of materials, open-source software costs, or comparisons with frugal alternatives and high-end systems. The OT-2 Nucleic Acid Extraction Workstation cost $11,340. Using 24-sample runs, manual extraction required approximately 5 hours of hands-on technician time, compared with 1.5 hours for the OT-2, saving 3.5 hours per run. At an assumed throughput of 500 samples per month and a technician wage of $30/hour, the authors estimate 72.92 hours and $2,187.60 in monthly FTE savings, recovering the initial investment in approximately five months (described elsewhere as less than six months). The system processed eight samples in under one hour and 96 samples in under three hours on average; fastest kits required 25 minutes for eight samples and 1.5 hours for 96. Across multiple extraction kits and sample types, it produced comparable yields to manual procedures while improving reproducibility and precision. More than 95% successful qPCR detection met EUA criterion-level performance, and the excerpt reports greater than 96% of samples passed for every kit across 22 samples. These figures should be classified as an all-in workstation investment and labor-payback estimate, not a component-level BOM.

contexts.context: The excerpt supports the cost and conceptual framing of low-cost laboratory automation. It identifies the Opentrons OT-2 as having an approximately USD 7,500 starting cost, while noting that whether it counts as consumables, spare resources, or dedicated support depends on the institution and use case. The review defines a “frugal twin” as a low-cost counterpart to a higher-cost physical laboratory system. Frugal twins are intended to provide lower-risk environments for rapid prototyping and education, while offering insights relevant to more expensive systems. Their usefulness lies on a trade-off spectrum between cost and research capability. Cost reduction can be achieved either by reducing capabilities or by accepting lower accuracy and precision; the appropriate balance depends on available resources and required functions. Table 1 lists a “Cheap automated synthesis platform” for chemistry and organic synthesis at an estimated cost of USD 450, illustrating that a component or platform-level low-cost estimate can be substantially below the OT-2 starting price. The excerpt does not provide the requested later-source results concerning OT-2 protein throughput, AutoLab adoption, cell-culture labor savings, OT-Mation CSV-to-Python workflows, integration standards, or specific bill-of-materials versus all-in cost distinctions. It therefore supports only the OT-2, frugal-twin, and USD 450 platform portions of the requested comparison.

contexts.context: The excerpt documents Roche’s deep integration of the low-cost Opentrons OT-2 with its AutoLab workflow-orchestration software. Unlike a shallow integration, which transfers a worklist or input sheet while leaving the user to operate the manufacturer’s software, deep integration uses a device-specific API and allows external software to control the liquid handler without manual initiation or monitoring. Roche presents this architecture as a way to reduce onboarding difficulty, simplify workflows, reduce manual errors, support FAIR data practices, and improve flexibility and reliability in pharmaceutical research. The article identifies industrial adoption barriers including the cost of advanced automation systems, limited laboratory space, insufficient in-house expertise for script development and maintenance, and negative prior experiences with automation suppliers. It also records important OT-2 limitations: restricted deck space, no plate transport, an eight-channel maximum pipetting head, no liquid-level detection, and software shortcomings such as absent built-in user dialogs and limited variable handling. The supplied pages do not provide a specific OT-2 purchase price, bill of materials, all-in deployment cost, or quantitative adoption/throughput results. They also do not mention the other cited studies, such as Lo, Doloi, Norton-Baker, Courville, or Laverick, nor provide a specific SiLA implementation.

contexts.context: Courville et al. (2025) describe the Automated Cell Culture Splitter (ACCS), an open-source automation platform based on a minimally modified Opentrons OT-2, a temperature-controlled heat block, and a custom Cell Counting Imager (CCI) with a flow cell. The CCI performs on-deck imaging-based counting of samples from source-plate wells, allowing the system to compensate for well-to-well density differences and adjust seeding volumes on a per-well basis. The stated operational result is a reduction in hands-on time per plate by more than half relative to manual culture, while maintaining comparable accuracy and biological outcomes. A single installation can passage approximately 2–3 source plates per working day, with minimal or no intervention after starting a run. The compact system can fit in a biosafety cabinet and is intended to be adaptable to other applications. Hardware designs, software source code, and builder documentation were released under open-source licenses, supporting reuse and modification. However, this excerpt provides no dollar figures, component bill of materials, or all-in installation cost, so it cannot substantiate comparisons such as OT-2 purchase price, frugal-twin cost, 3D-printing expense, or total system cost. (SLAS Technology 29, 2024, 100180) report that integrating the low-cost, modular Opentrons OT-2 with AutoLab’s workflow orchestration, HTTP API, and open-source networking tools reduced development time, training, and errors. A validated metabolite-identification assay achieved an intraclass correlation coefficient of 0.998 versus manual execution, while replicate variation averaged less than one-third of manual results. Automation saved 30 minutes per assay and halved labor cost, but did not recoup hardware costs within five years; reusing workflows and running multiple assays could accelerate break-even.

answer.formatted_answer:
Question: What do market reports and academic studies show about the laboratory automation and self-driving laboratory market: market size and growth, business models (instrument sales, software, cloud labs, services), outcomes of cloud-lab companies (Emerald Cloud Lab, Strateos/Transcriptic), Opentrons, and the role of open-source hardware and software in adoption and cost? Give numbers with years and sources.

# Laboratory automation and self-driving laboratories: market evidence

**Bottom line.** There is a substantial, established market for *clinical* laboratory automation, but it should not be presented as the market for research self-driving laboratories (SDLs). The accessible market reports and studies document growing research activity, operating cloud labs, and useful commercial instruments; they do **not** establish a defensible stand-alone global SDL revenue figure, SDL growth rate, or profitability for the named private companies. (nam2025revolutionizinglaboratorypractices pages 2-4, nam2025revolutionizinglaboratorypractices pages 11-12, jung2025researchtrendanalysis pages 25-26, zilgalvis2025yingchiangjeffreylee pages 12-14)

## Size, growth, and the measurement boundary

Nam and Park’s 2025 clinical-laboratory review puts the **2023 global total laboratory automation (TLA) systems market at US$5.57–6.1 billion**. TLA here means automation across clinical specimen handling, testing, and post-analytical processes—not AI-directed research experiments. Their references identify a **QYResearch report updated June 2024**, covering 2024–2030, and a **Precedence Research report updated August 2024**, covering 2024–2034. The accessible material does not reproduce a verifiable forecast dollar value or CAGR from those reports; assigning one to the SDL segment would be unjustified. (nam2025revolutionizinglaboratorypractices pages 2-4, nam2025revolutionizinglaboratorypractices pages 11-12)

The same review reports **115 South Korean institutions operating TLA in 2024**, including **36 of 47 tertiary hospitals (77%)** and **58 of 331 general hospitals (18%)**. Its market-share figure puts **North America at 38%** and depicts **Siemens, Roche, and Beckman Coulter at 34%, 31%, and 25%**, respectively, in the reported clinical-automation vendor breakdown. These illustrate adoption and concentration within the *clinical* category, not an SDL company ranking. (nam2025revolutionizinglaboratorypractices pages 2-4, nam2025revolutionizinglaboratorypractices media 099f385e)

Research activity is growing, but it is a different metric: Jung and colleagues analyzed **352 SDL papers published during 2004–2023** and found a marked rise after **2019**. A 2025 study surveying publicly identifiable cloud labs found **15 example organizations worldwide**, explicitly **not** an exhaustive census. Neither publications nor provider counts measure revenue. (jung2025researchtrendanalysis pages 25-26, zilgalvis2025yingchiangjeffreylee pages 12-14, zilgalvis2025yingchiangjeffreylee pages 9-12)

The following comparison keeps market revenue, research activity, access commitments, and equipment prices separate.

| Metric | Dated value | What it measures / limitation | Source |
|---|---:|---|---|
| Global clinical total laboratory automation (TLA) systems market | **$5.57–6.1 billion (2023)** | End-to-end automation of clinical-laboratory pre-analytical, analytical, and post-analytical processes—not the research self-driving-laboratory (SDL) market. The cited market sources were QYResearch, updated June 2024, and Precedence Research, updated August 2024; no verified CAGR appears in the accessible excerpts. | Nam & Park (2025) (nam2025revolutionizinglaboratorypractices pages 2-4, nam2025revolutionizinglaboratorypractices pages 11-12) |
| SDL research activity | **352 publications, 2004–2023** | Web of Science bibliometric count; publications surged after 2019. **Not market revenue, installed systems, or company sales.** | Jung et al. (2025) (jung2025researchtrendanalysis pages 25-26) |
| Emerald Cloud Lab access commitment | **More than $250,000** | Reported minimum financial commitment for ECL access. This is a secondary-review figure whose pricing basis and inclusions were not independently verified; it is neither company revenue nor a standardized SDL price. | Doloi et al. (2025) (doloi2025democratizingselfdrivinglabs pages 4-6) |
| Opentrons OT-2 starting cost | **Approximately $7,500 (2024 review)** | Starting platform price, not a complete workflow including modules, pipettes, peripherals, integration, validation, consumables, maintenance, and labor. | Lo et al. (2024) (lo2024reviewoflowcost pages 5-6, lo2023reviewoflowcost pages 2-5) |
| Opentrons OT-2 entry-level estimate | **Approximately $10,000 (2025 review)** | Indicative entry-level liquid-handler cost; configuration and publication-date differences help explain why it exceeds the $7,500 starting estimate. | Doloi et al. (2025) (doloi2025democratizingselfdrivinglabs pages 6-7) |
| Configured Opentrons OT-2 system | **Approximately $20,000–30,000 (2024)** | OT-2 with pipettes and accessory modules for protein expression and purification; closer to a configured system than a bare starting price, but not necessarily full lifetime cost. | Norton-Baker et al. (2024) (nortonbaker2024enablinghighthroughputenzyme pages 1-2) |
| Open-source FINDUS liquid handler | **Under $400 construction cost (2025 review)** | Build/component cost for a customizable 3D-printed workstation; excludes builder labor, calibration, maintenance, integration, and possibly ancillary equipment. Reported pipetting error was below 0.3%. | Doloi et al. (2025) (doloi2025democratizingselfdrivinglabs pages 9-10) |
| Higher-end commercial liquid handlers | **More than $60,000; some capable systems more than $150,000** | Broad, non-like-for-like comparison: Doloi et al. place high-end integrated platforms above $60,000, while Norton-Baker et al. report Hamilton/Tecan systems with the required capabilities above $150,000. | Doloi et al. (2025); Norton-Baker et al. (2024) (doloi2025democratizingselfdrivinglabs pages 6-7, nortonbaker2024enablinghighthroughputenzyme pages 1-2) |


*Table: Comparison of market, publication, access, and equipment-cost figures that are frequently conflated. The table separates clinical TLA revenue from SDL research activity and distinguishes starting prices from configured or component-level costs.*

## How the businesses capture value

* **Instruments and integration.** Manufacturers sell liquid handlers, modules, analytical instruments, consumables, and support. A robot is not itself an SDL: experiment-selection algorithms, instrument interfaces, scheduling, measurements, and data infrastructure must close the loop. In 2024, Roche researchers integrated an **Opentrons OT-2** with their in-house **AutoLab** orchestration software using the robot’s API, illustrating why instrument sales and the integration/software layer are distinct sources of value. (thieme2024deepintegrationof pages 1-2, thieme2024deepintegrationof pages 5-6)
* **Software.** Protocol-generation, orchestration, sample tracking, analysis, and data management can be developed internally, distributed openly, or supplied commercially. The open-source **OT-Mation** project, published in **2025**, converts experimental-design CSV files into executable OT-2 Python protocols; it demonstrates a software complement to purchased hardware, not evidence of software-market revenue. (laverick2025otmationanopensource pages 1-2)
* **Cloud labs and services.** A provider operates expensive physical facilities while customers remotely specify experiments and obtain measurements and records; charges may combine access commitments and usage. Academic authors distinguish **Emerald Cloud Lab’s (ECL’s)** broad instrument-access approach from **Strateos’s** predefined workflows emphasizing drug discovery and synthetic biology. A 2025 review reports an **ECL minimum financial commitment exceeding US$250,000**, but this secondary-source figure is not independently verified pricing or ECL revenue. Moving capital spending from customer to provider does not eliminate infrastructure or operating costs. (arias2024scientificdiscoveryat pages 2-2, doloi2025democratizingselfdrivinglabs pages 4-6, doloi2025democratizingselfdrivinglabs pages 6-7, arias2024scientificdiscoveryat pages 8-8)

## What happened at the named companies

**Emerald Cloud Lab.** A 2025 cloud-lab landscape report lists ECL’s Austin facility at **105,000 ft² and more than 230 instruments**; it lists the ECL–Carnegie Mellon facility at **20,000 ft² and more than 200 instruments**. Its **2021** CMU entry refers to the announced project, **not proof that it was fully operational in 2021**. More concretely, a **2025** published study remotely performed copper-nanocluster experiments at ECL in Austin and CMU’s automated laboratory in Pittsburgh, using different handlers and spectrometers across sites; models trained on **40 samples** predicted successful synthesis. This demonstrates research use and cross-site validation, not ECL profitability or a measured company-wide productivity gain. (zilgalvis2025yingchiangjeffreylee pages 12-14, montoyagonzalez2025crosslaboratoryvalidationof pages 1-2)

**Strateos/Transcriptic.** Strateos emerged from the **Transcriptic–3Scan merger**; the landscape report lists a **14,000-ft² facility and approximately 200 instruments** under its **2019** company entry. Its original remote, workflow-oriented offering was followed by an announced shift toward **on-site cloud labs**, reported in academic discussion in **2024**. A substantive operating example is the DARPA SD2 *Round Trip* project: its open software was integrated with the **Strateos robotic cloud laboratory** and, by the **2022** paper, had been applied to **nearly 100 experiments**. The authors report roughly **two orders of magnitude faster experimental design and analysis** than prior ad hoc processes and describe a project-workflow staffing comparison of approximately **ten versus three people**. Those are results for the **combined software and experimental workflow**; they do not isolate a Strateos-only effect or establish Strateos revenue, margins, or profitability. (zilgalvis2025yingchiangjeffreylee pages 12-14, arias2024scientificdiscoveryat pages 8-8, bryce2022roundtripan pages 9-10, bryce2022roundtripan pages 3-4, bryce2022roundtripan pages 1-2)

**Opentrons.** Its commercially sold, programmable OT-2 offers a lower-cost route to *in-house* automation rather than remote access to a provider’s lab. Published indicative prices differ with date and configuration: approximately **US$7,500 starting cost** in a **2024** review; about **US$10,000** as a **2025** review’s entry-level estimate; and approximately **US$20,000–30,000** with pipettes and accessory modules for a **2024** protein-workflow study. In that study, researchers processed **96 proteins in parallel**, with a proposed capacity of hundreds per user per week. These are product and application figures, **not** Opentrons sales, market share, or profits. (lo2023reviewoflowcost pages 2-5, doloi2025democratizingselfdrivinglabs pages 6-7, nortonbaker2024enablinghighthroughputenzyme pages 1-2)

The industrial economics are instructive. Roche’s **2024** OT-2/AutoLab study reports **30 minutes less hands-on work per MetID assay**, approximately **half the labor cost per sample**, agreement with manual results of **ICC 0.998**, and replicate variability averaging **less than one-third** of the manual procedure’s. Nevertheless, at the studied assay volume the authors say the labor saving **did not fully offset hardware usage within five years**; sharing the machine across workflows might improve payback. This is stronger evidence than assuming every affordable robot rapidly pays for itself. (thieme2024deepintegrationof pages 5-6)

The landscape report cautions that provider facility measurements can include offices, instrument counts are reported inconsistently, and much information comes from company statements. The retrieved evidence supplies **no independently verified annual revenue, customer counts, profitability, valuation outcome, or definitive exit outcome** for ECL, Strateos, or Opentrons. Facility scale, funding or a published experiment should not be substituted for those business outcomes. (zilgalvis2025yingchiangjeffreylee pages 12-14, zilgalvis2025yingchiangjeffreylee pages 20-25)

## Open source: adoption benefits and cost limits

Open designs and code let labs modify instruments, share protocols, and build applications atop a purchased platform. Illustrations include the **2025** OT-Mation software; the **2025** open-source OT-2 cell-culture system that cut hands-on plate-passaging time by **more than half** in its reported tests; and a **2025** review’s account of the 3D-printed **FINDUS** liquid handler costing **under US$400 to construct**. The latter is a *construction* figure, not a like-for-like quotation for a validated, serviced commercial workstation. A 2024 review also describes a roughly **US$450** educational synthesis platform as a “frugal twin”: useful for learning and prototyping, but potentially less capable or precise than the research system it approximates. (laverick2025otmationanopensource pages 1-2, courville2025opensourcecellculture pages 1-2, doloi2025democratizingselfdrivinglabs pages 9-10, lo2024reviewoflowcost pages 5-6)

Openness does not remove the cost of calibration, skilled integration, analytical instruments, consumables, quality control, or maintenance. Roche notes the OT-2’s limited deck space, absence of plate transport and liquid-level detection, and eight-channel maximum head. A **2026 preprint** further argues that incompatible instrument-control conventions cause labs to rebuild integrations even when orchestration software is open source. Thus, open hardware and software plausibly lower the **entry price and reuse cost**, while validated interoperability and sufficient instrument utilization determine whether they lower the **cost per reliable result**. (thieme2024deepintegrationof pages 1-2, lo2024reviewoflowcost pages 5-6, gottstein2026talkingtoinstruments pages 1-4, thieme2024deepintegrationof pages 5-6)

**Assessment:** The demonstrated opportunity spans several different businesses—clinical automation equipment, research instruments, workflow software, and experiment-as-a-service. Published case studies substantiate technical utility and some workflow savings. They do **not**, on the evidence available here, substantiate a precise SDL market CAGR or the financial success of the three private companies. (nam2025revolutionizinglaboratorypractices pages 2-4, jung2025researchtrendanalysis pages 25-26, zilgalvis2025yingchiangjeffreylee pages 12-14, thieme2024deepintegrationof pages 5-6)
